generatedProse.concept-context: Reflective writing is a staple of training across the School of Sport: clinic logs, placement portfolios, coaching diaries and reflective commentaries all call for it, and it is marked. Because it focuses on your own experience, it tempts the writer into narration. Critical reflective writing in sport does more: it evaluates your own actions, weighs them against professional and ethical standards, points to evidence from the episode, and ends in a justified plan for development. The difference between a pass and a strong reflective piece is almost always the move from telling the story to judging it.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport therapy students write a reflective entry about the same event: a home exercise programme they gave a patient that the patient did not keep to.

Tom writes: I explained the exercises clearly and gave the patient a printed sheet to follow. The patient did not keep to the programme. I was disappointed, but I respected their choice and moved on. This is faithful narration. It reports the sequence and a feeling, but it never asks whether the programme or the way it was explained could have been better, and it reaches no conclusion about Tom's own practice.

Amara writes: I prescribed the exercises, but on reflection I built the programme around what I thought was best rather than the patient's routine and goals. Guidance on patient-centred rehabilitation suggests building the plan around the patient's own priorities and capacity. Next time I will ask about routine and barriers before prescribing. This evaluates Amara's own actions against a professional standard and justifies a specific change.

Both described the event. Only Amara produced critical reflective writing: evaluative, evidenced, and ending in a justified plan.
generatedProse.summary: Across the School of Sport, critical reflective writing evaluates your own actions rather than narrating them: it weighs what you did against professional and ethical standards, cites evidence from the episode, and justifies a plan for development. You can now write reflection that judges rather than tells, support your conclusions with evidence, and appraise a reflective piece against professional criteria. You now have the stance, the structure and the writing to sustain reflective practice as a sport professional.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's conclusion justified rather than merely asserted?

items.text: She weighed her own approach against patient-centred rehabilitation and pointed to evidence from the episode.
She stated her plan more confidently than Tom did.
She described the patient's reaction in more detail.
She wrote the entry in the first person.

feedback.correct: That's right. Weighing her actions against a professional standard and citing evidence is what justifies the conclusion.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara offered in support of her conclusion.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara's conclusion was justified because she weighed her approach against patient-centred rehabilitation and pointed to evidence, not because it was confident, detailed or first-person.
